note: Expected rows for the two final plan strategies. Generated from the real code, so these are what it produces today. Only the columns that carry the decision are listed; the gauge, temper and shape columns are copied from the per order plan unchanged.

conventions.CoilNo: A coil no is issued only where the coil DIVIDES, and both halves are CHILDREN of the coil being divided: rod FW7001 divides into FW7001A and FW7001B, and FW7001B divides again into FW7001BA and FW7001BB. Where nothing divides, the arriving coil no carries through. A coil no is a six character root plus at most three alphas, so at nine characters GenerateCoilAlpha carries on from the letter after the first alpha and strips the rest - the children of FW7005BBB are FW7005C and FW7005D. An output going BACK TO STOCK is asked for with wareHouseAlpha = 1 instead, which generates from LEFT(parent, 6), giving a coil at the rod's own level rather than under the coil it came off.
conventions.Weights: WeightOn and WeightOff are the weight of the coil the operation RECEIVES: the whole rod at the first flatten, the balance at each later flatten, and the order's own planned weight once its piece has been peeled off. RequiredInWeight is the order's planned weight throughout.
conventions.OnGaugeWeight: On a piece row it is the order's planned weight. On a balance row it is the total still to be planned, which is the weight handed to the next flatten.
conventions.NextOperation: FlatLineProcessing has no next operation column. That a balance is flattened again is expressed by its CoilNo arriving at a routing whose OperationLetter is F - so FW7001B leaves the first flatten and arrives at the second.
conventions.Levels: LevelId is unique across the plan and ParentLevelId chains each order's first flatten to the flatten its balance came from, so the cascade is one tree.
conventions.MfgOrderNo: 0 everywhere. It is assigned when the plan is exported, not when it is planned.
conventions.BackToStock: A stock order's material goes back to stock at its LAST output, and that row carries the flag. The merge has to invent an as is flatten to hold it when the order finishes at the anneal, because the furnace output cannot be divided; the cascade does not, because the order already has an output row of its own. Either way the coil that row travels on is asked for with wareHouseAlpha = 1.

openPoints: A root operation row carries no weight in this sample because the row itself is synthetic here. In production it is written by the root operation and carries the rod weight, which both strategies pass through untouched.

The LAST order carries the balance coil it arrived on rather than a fresh alpha, because nothing divides at its flatten - in the three order case order 123458 travels on FW7001BB. Its own first flatten therefore reads as a no op on the flat line, FW7001BB to FW7001BB, for the same 800 lb the balance row above it already reported. Both operations are real - one is the previous order's flatten, one is its own - but the pair looks duplicated. Confirm, or say the last order should get its own alpha too.

The first flatten's WeightOn is the WHOLE rod (3,000) even though only the leading order's 1,000 lb comes off it as finished output. This matches the merge, where a shared operation carries the pre division weight. Confirm rather than the 1,000 lb.

Under BalanceToPiece each order gets its OWN flatten operation at the flat line, so a three order rod plans three FL1 operations. That is the check out and check in the client described. The merge plans one.

scenarios.name: Three orders on one rod - the worked cascade
scenarios.description: The case the request states: a 3,000 lb rod, order one needing 1,000 lb and two more orders sharing the rest. Each flatten peels one order off and hands the balance on.

scenarios.name: Two orders - a single split
scenarios.description: The smallest cascade. One split, so two pieces and no balance that is flattened twice.

scenarios.name: One order - nothing divides
scenarios.description: A single order divides nothing, so no alpha is issued and the rod keeps its own coil no through every operation. Both strategies must agree here.

scenarios.name: Four orders - the cascade nests three deep
scenarios.description: Each division produces children of the coil arriving, so the alphas nest: A and B, then BA and BB, then BBA and BBB. A coil no is a six character root plus at most three alphas, which is exactly the depth three divisions need.

scenarios.name: Five orders - the fourth division has no room to nest
scenarios.description: A fourth division would need a tenth character, so GenerateCoilAlpha carries on from the letter after the first alpha and strips the rest: the children of FW7005BBB are seven character coil nos again. This is the one case where a piece is not a descendant of the coil it came off, and the generator decides it, not the planner.

scenarios.name: Part of the rod is left unplanned
scenarios.description: 1,000 and 800 planned on a 3,000 lb rod. The balance carries what is still to be PLANNED, not what is left on the rod, so the 1,200 lb remainder appears nowhere and is left as it is.

scenarios.name: Flattens only - an FL3 route with no spool stage
scenarios.description: No anneal, so the route is a single flatten on FL3 and there is no spool stage at all. The split still happens at that flatten.

scenarios.name: A root operation was added first
scenarios.description: The planner added a root operation, so a blank order no row sits at sequence 0 level 1 and every order's chain starts from that offset.

scenarios.name: Mixed routes - one order ends on a flatten, the other on an anneal
scenarios.description: Order one is FAF and order two is FA, so under the merge they diverge at the anneal and an extra as-is flatten has to be written for the order that is already finished. Under the cascade each order has its own chain from the start, so nothing diverges and no as-is flatten is needed. Compare the IsAsIs rows.

scenarios.name: An as is stock order goes back to stock
scenarios.description: Order two is a stock order finishing at the anneal, so the merge creates an as is flatten to separate it and its output goes BACK TO STOCK. Its coil no is asked for as a warehouse alpha, which GetCoilAlpha generates from the rod rather than from the coil it came off, because material going back to stock becomes a stock coil in its own right. Under the cascade each order has its own chain, so no as is flatten is needed and the piece itself is the back to stock output.
